study. AI-assisted, with professional judgement and review.<\/p><\/aside><div id=\"navBackdrop\" class=\"nav-backdrop\"><\/div><div class=\"page-frame report-frame\"><main class=\"shell report\" id=\"mainContent\"><p class=\"report-kicker\">Jonathan Pincher · Design rationale · Project sketch<\/p><div class=\"section-guide-band\"><h1 id=\"page-heading\">Instructional design and user interface considerations<\/h1><div class=\"page-avatar-slot\"><div id=\"avatarWrap\" aria-hidden=\"true\"><\/div><\/div><\/div><p class=\"report-lead\">Start with a stick. Change the audience. See how much of the design needs to change with it.<\/p><p>I built this project to make my design thinking visible. Rather than describe an approach in the abstract, I created a start-to-finish online learning package around a fictional need and two real-world student groups: 15-year-old school learners and first-year undergraduates.<\/p><p>The material is deliberately ordinary. The design questions are more demanding. What should each group be able to do? How much support is useful? What does a tutor need to teach, assess and respond? What would an institution need before adopting the package? Those questions connect curriculum development with the details of the experience, right down to the wording on a button.<\/p><p>This section focuses on instructional design and user interface: how I turn those questions into structure, explanation, interaction and feedback. The separate <a href=\"learning-curriculum-design.html#curriculum-title\">Curriculum design<\/a> section explores that dimension of the project. I encourage you to look at both: the curriculum establishes the intended journey, and the experience has to make that journey workable.<\/p><p>I consider the interface part of that design thinking. It is where a person encounters the instructions, chooses a route, operates the model and interprets the response. I therefore examine the content and the controls together: what needs explaining, what should be immediately visible, what can wait until it is requested, and how someone recognises their next action. A sound activity can still be difficult to use if its interface creates uncertainty. In this project, the wording, visual hierarchy, navigation, control placement and feedback are all opportunities to make the intended experience easier to understand and operate.<\/p><p>Think of this as a working sketch of my approach. There is enough here to explore choices and inspect the reasoning behind them. It is not a finished programme, a commissioned institutional solution or evidence of improved learning outcomes. Part of good design is knowing what a prototype can show—and what still needs to be tested.<\/p>\n<div class=\"section-guide-actions\"><details><summary id=\"sectionGuideRead\">Read spoken introduction<\/summary><p id=\"sectionGuideTranscript\"><\/p><\/details><\/div><section id=\"addie\"><h2 id=\"nav-section-1\">ADDIE — how I examine the design process<\/h2><p>ADDIE stands for <strong>Analyse, Design, Develop, Implement and Evaluate<\/strong>. It gives us a useful way to explain the work behind an experience. I am using it here to make the process inspectable, rather than claim that every stage has been completed in this sketch.<\/p><span class=\"illustration-plan-marker\" id=\"illustration-37\" aria-hidden=\"true\"><\/span><p>I would not treat the stages as a one-way production line. A prototype may reveal that the analysis was incomplete; feedback may send me back to a design decision. My test, test, test approach belongs throughout the work.<\/p><p>Select a stage or its arrow to see how I approached it in this project. Select it again to close it. You can open several stages at once.<\/p><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"addie-stage-1\"><summary>Analyse — understand the need before choosing the solution<\/summary><div><p>I started with a fictional need and two recognisable student groups, then considered the learner, tutor and institutional perspectives. That creates a basis for the two pathways. It does not replace discovery with a real commissioner: prior knowledge, barriers, delivery constraints and success criteria would need confirming with the people involved.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"addie-stage-2\"><summary>Design — decide how the experience should work<\/summary><div><p>I organised the routes, resources and supporting explanation, and considered how visitors would predict, investigate and interpret a result. The twenty broader criteria and the screen-design considerations make those choices visible. The curriculum account will examine the relationship between outcomes, activities and assessment in more depth.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"addie-stage-3\"><summary>Develop — build enough to test the decisions<\/summary><div><p>I developed working pages, the model, the supporting resources and recorded introductions. Building exposed problems that a written plan alone would not reveal: disappearing geometry, unstable layout and language-dependent navigation. Revising those details is part of development, not simply tidying up after it.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"addie-stage-4\"><summary>Implement — put it into its intended setting<\/summary><div><p>The prototype can be explored, but it has not been implemented as a course within an institution. A real implementation would include an agreed delivery environment, tutor preparation, learner support, access arrangements and ownership of updates. Making a file available is not the same as making a learning experience work in practice.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"addie-stage-5\"><summary>Evaluate — find out what works and what needs to change<\/summary><div><p>Owner reviews and implementation checks have informed this sketch. Independent usability work, learner outcomes, stakeholder feedback and evidence from use in an institution remain to be gathered. I would use those findings to revisit earlier decisions, keeping the successful parts while investigating the sticking points.<\/p><\/div><\/details><p><strong>The useful connection:<\/strong> ADDIE describes stages of work; the criteria help me question decisions within that work; observation and feedback help me judge the result. None of those should be mistaken for proof that this prototype has succeeded with its intended audiences.<\/p><a class=\"report-back\" href=\"#report-index\">Back to index ↑<\/a><\/section><section id=\"experience-and-standards\"><h2 id=\"nav-section-2\">Good principles are the start of the conversation<\/h2><p>There are many published standards and sources of guidance available to designers. Examples include <a href=\"https://www.iso.org/standard/75258.html\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener\">ISO 9241-110 on interaction principles<\/a>, <a href=\"https://www.iso.org/standard/77520.html\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener\">ISO 9241-210 on human-centred design<\/a>, <a href=\"https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener\">W3C WCAG 2.2 accessibility guidelines<\/a>, <a href=\"https://www.nngroup.com/articles/ten-usability-heuristics/\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener\">Nielsen’s ten usability heuristics<\/a> and the <a href=\"https://design-system.service.gov.uk/\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener\">GOV.UK Design System<\/a>. I include these as examples of the wider landscape, not as a list of frameworks I personally use or a claim that this project complies with them.<\/p><p>Published guidance can help a designer ask better questions about what an experience needs to achieve and why. Some sources also offer practical help with how. What they cannot do is choose the right solution for every combination of people, purpose and setting. That is where experience and application matter: developing something, seeing where it works, finding the sticking points and being willing to change it.<\/p><p>Working across different needs, users and institutions develops judgement. It also gives me more assumptions to question, not fewer. A solution that worked in one setting is a possibility to explore in the next—not a reason to stop listening.<\/p><p>That understanding really developed through my work at <a href=\"#experience-skillkit\">Skillkit<\/a>, the <a href=\"#experience-miid\">Manchester Institute for Information Delivery at Manchester Metropolitan University<\/a> and <a href=\"#experience-idea\">IDEA, where I was founding Chair<\/a>. Across that work, I was designing for diverse groups of learners and supporting SMEs to develop their businesses and accelerate growth, sometimes without knowing in advance exactly who would use a product or what support they would need. I could not rely on my own view of how it ought to work. Feedback from students and administrators was essential to fine-tuning the products in use: understanding what was helping, where people were getting stuck and what needed to change. Those experiences taught me to treat a design as something to keep learning from once it reaches the people it is meant to serve.<\/p><details class=\"graphic-consideration cv-excerpt\" id=\"experience-skillkit\"><summary>Skillkit Ltd — view CV section<\/summary><div><h3 id=\"nav-section-3\">Skillkit Ltd<\/h3><p><strong>Founder &amp; Owner · 1997–2014<\/strong><\/p><ul><li>Built Skillkit from inception to approximately £1 million annual revenue, establishing a business delivering online education and skills programmes.<\/li><li>Established online and blended learning programmes and LMS/VLE delivery, managing the full cycle from needs analysis and design to evaluation.<\/li><li>Developed staff for increased responsibility through management, mentoring and practical experience, supporting future leader development.<\/li><li>Refined programme content and learner-support processes using learner feedback, progress monitoring and performance information.<\/li><li>Created client-management systems covering enquiries, learner support and accurate records, producing evidence for UK and European government audits.<\/li><li>Coordinated digital learning projects, government contracts, European funding proposals and budgets, balancing delivery priorities with reporting requirements.<\/li><\/ul><p class=\"small\">Extract from Jonathan Pincher’s Blended Learning Designer CV, page 1. Only the relevant employment entry is shown.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration cv-excerpt\" id=\"experience-miid\"><summary>Manchester Institute for Information Delivery — view CV section<\/summary><div><h3 id=\"nav-section-4\">Manchester Institute for Information Delivery<\/h3><p><strong>Founder &amp; Director · 1996–2007 · Manchester Metropolitan University<\/strong><\/p><ul><li>Built and led a university-based institute recruiting and training approximately 6,000 learners annually, taking provision from course design through delivery.<\/li><li>Secured formal FEFC accreditation for courses personally designed and written, enabling access to Further Education Funding Council funding.<\/li><li>Translated employer and learner needs into complete courses, with defined learning outcomes, curricula, delivery methods and assessments.<\/li><li>Established partnerships across four countries—the UK, Spain, Finland and China—supporting international education and skills-development collaboration.<\/li><li>Trained and mentored university staff and brought academic, technical and operational teams together to deliver multidisciplinary programmes.<\/li><li>Improved delivery processes using input from clients, colleagues and partners, streamlining activity and reducing unnecessary overheads.<\/li><li>Maintained accreditation evidence, programme records and formal FEFC reporting, demonstrating accountability for externally funded learning delivery.<\/li><\/ul><p class=\"small\">Extract from Jonathan Pincher’s Blended Learning Designer CV, page 2. Only the relevant employment entry is shown.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration cv-excerpt\" id=\"experience-idea\"><summary>IDEA — view CV section<\/summary><div><h3 id=\"nav-section-5\">IDEA<\/h3><p><strong>Founding Chair<\/strong><\/p><ul><li>Helped identify and train SMEs, supporting them to develop their businesses and accelerate growth.<\/li><li>Successfully positioned participating companies within the creative industries in the North West of England.<\/li><\/ul><\/div><\/details><p><strong>My mantra is simple: test, test, test. Are my assumptions correct?<\/strong> Can people find their way? Do they understand what happened? Where do they hesitate, and what did they expect instead? I want to see the experience through their actions and hear their account of it, rather than rely on my own familiarity with the design.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-6\">And then there is the X factor<\/h3><p>Does the product feel inviting? Is there some pleasure in using it? Do people want to explore, participate and come back when it is useful? Those questions matter to me. They are not completely absent from established design thinking, but they cannot be answered by a checklist alone.<\/p><p>In this project, the responsive experiment, a guide with a clear role and small, consistent moments of feedback are ways of exploring that experience. They are design propositions, not proof of enjoyment. I would investigate them through observation, conversation and feedback: what feels satisfying, what becomes irritating, what people choose to use, and why. More clicks or more time on a page could mean interest—or confusion. I need the context before drawing a conclusion.<\/p><p>Once a product is in use, the learning continues. I would bring together user and tutor feedback, support questions and proportionate usage information, then look for patterns worth investigating. I want to protect the parts that work and improve the parts that get in the way. For this sketch, that field evidence has not yet been collected; the next step is to put the assumptions in front of representative users and stakeholders.<\/p><\/section>\n<h2 id=\"nav-section-7\">How I make design decisions<\/h2><p>The twenty criteria below help me turn that approach into decisions. I apply them to the instructional experience and its interface, using each as a question to explore rather than a box to tick. For each one, I explain why it matters, what I did here and what I want to find out. The point is to make my thinking visible—and open to challenge.<\/p><p>I distinguish intention from evidence throughout. A clear rationale explains why something should work. Testing with the people who will use, teach and support it is how I find out whether it does.<\/p><div class=\"report-index\" id=\"report-index\"><h2 id=\"nav-section-8\">Design criteria and their application<\/h2><p>Select a heading or its arrow to expand the explanation, see how I applied the criterion and what I want it to achieve. Select it again to close it. You can open several criteria and explore them in any order.<\/p><span class=\"illustration-plan-marker\" id=\"illustration-39\" aria-hidden=\"true\"><\/span><\/div><div class=\"graphic-index-columns instructional-index-columns\"><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"criterion-1\"><summary>01 Purpose and intended outcome<\/summary><div><h3 id=\"nav-section-9\">Why it matters to me<\/h3><p>I begin by defining what someone should understand, decide or be able to do. Without an explicit outcome, an experience can become a collection of attractive features whose contribution is difficult to judge. The intended outcome gives me a basis for choosing content, interaction and evidence of success.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-10\">How I applied it<\/h3><p>I set the brief around two things a visitor should be able to inspect: a coherent online learning package and the decisions that shaped it. That meant developing learner activities alongside teaching packs, tutor views, comparison and reflection, rather than presenting an isolated animation. I then made the instructional design and user interface account a primary opening-page choice alongside the courses. For an employer, that creates a direct route to the evidence most relevant to their interest: the experience itself or my reasoning behind it. I kept the detailed account in its own section so demonstrating depth does not require every visitor to read it.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-11\">What I want this to achieve<\/h3><p>I separated experience from detailed rationale so visitors can explore first and inspect my reasoning when it is relevant. I would assess success by whether they can explain the purpose of the experience and the reason for its different pathways.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"criterion-2\"><summary>02 Audience and context<\/summary><div><h3 id=\"nav-section-12\">Why it matters to me<\/h3><p>I need to understand who will use a design, what they already know and the conditions in which they will encounter it. Those factors shape language, depth, pacing and the amount of support. A design that ignores context can be clear to its author and confusing to its intended audience.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-13\">How I applied it<\/h3><p>I held the topic constant and changed the demands placed on the two groups. The school route emphasises observation, prediction, fair testing and an explanation grounded in evidence; the university route introduces modelling, uncertainty and the limits of a defensible conclusion. I made those groups explicit in the navigation and resources so visitors do not have to infer which version they are viewing. I also provided teaching packs and tutor views because the person delivering an activity needs a different view of it from the person completing it. This makes the audience distinction visible in the tasks and support, as well as in the labels.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-14\">What I want this to achieve<\/h3><p>Explicit audience labels help visitors choose a relevant route. Activities, teaching packs and tutor views offer different levels of detail. These are design responses to audience needs; direct observation is still needed to confirm that the vocabulary and support are appropriate.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"criterion-3\"><summary>03 Relevance and motivation<\/summary><div><h3 id=\"nav-section-15\">Why it matters to me<\/h3><p>I want people to recognise a reason to engage. Interest is useful when it brings attention to the intended question and encourages purposeful action. I judge an engaging feature by what it helps someone investigate, rather than by novelty alone.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-16\">How I applied it<\/h3><p>I used a familiar object to give the investigation an accessible entry point, then made its behaviour worth examining. The experiment lets visitors alter force, diameter, span and material setting and see a consequence. I added an illustrative snap at minimum diameter and maximum force to create a memorable event, but deliberately kept an explanation beside the scene: this trigger does not calculate real wood failure. That qualification matters because a more realistic-looking illustration can make an invented event appear authoritative. I wanted the drama to invite a question, with the model’s limits available at the moment the event is encountered.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-17\">What I want this to achieve<\/h3><p>I used the snap as an invitation to investigate extremes, with a nearby explanation that it is an invented trigger. This preserves interest while distinguishing the demonstration from a factual prediction of when real wood breaks.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"criterion-4\"><summary>04 Clear starting point<\/summary><div><h3 id=\"nav-section-18\">Why it matters to me<\/h3><p>I aim to make the first meaningful action apparent. If visitors must work out how the interface operates before they can understand its purpose, I have introduced an avoidable barrier. An effective starting point establishes the premise and offers a manageable choice.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-19\">How I applied it<\/h3><p>I gave the opening page two complementary jobs: establish the investigation and let visitors choose how to explore my work. The concise entry choices now put instructional design and user interface, curriculum design and the courses in view and give each route a developed destination. The original hero and prediction remain available for visitors who want a more experiential start. I kept the entry descriptions short and placed the substantial explanations in their destinations. The trade-off is between giving enough context to make a meaningful choice and adding so much introductory material that the visitor has to work before reaching the project.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-20\">What I want this to achieve<\/h3><p>The first choices relate to clear visitor intentions: inspect the approach or try it. I would test whether a first-time visitor can identify a suitable route without an explanation from me.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"criterion-5\"><summary>05 Information structure and sequence<\/summary><div><h3 id=\"nav-section-21\">Why it matters to me<\/h3><p>I organise information so people can build understanding in a sensible order and also find a specific item when they need it. Structure should make relationships visible and reduce dependence on memory.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-22\">How I applied it<\/h3><p>I arranged the numbered menu around recognisable purposes: overview, comparison, materials, activities, reflection and instructional design and user interface considerations. I separated the audience-specific teaching pathways from that main structure so the menu does not become a flat list of every resource. In this report, a clickable index offers direct access to each of the twenty criteria, with return links after the detail. That gives visitors both a suggested sequence and a way to inspect one question. I retained descriptive titles alongside numbers because the sequence alone cannot tell someone what a destination contains.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-23\">What I want this to achieve<\/h3><p>Numbering creates a recognisable route through the project without forcing everyone to follow it. Descriptive labels allow direct access, while this rationale sits after the practical experience as an optional deeper examination.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"criterion-6\"><summary>06 Manageable mental effort<\/summary><div><h3 id=\"nav-section-24\">Why it matters to me<\/h3><p>I try to reserve mental effort for the subject and the decision at hand. Interpreting an inconsistent interface, remembering hidden information or sorting through redundant messages consumes attention without advancing the intended outcome.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-25\">How I applied it<\/h3><p>I treated screen space and repeated messages as design costs. Oversized buttons were consuming vertical space without adding useful meaning, so I reduced their height while retaining wrapping for longer labels. In the experiment, I removed the Ready to test badge because it could be mistaken for a control and did not explain a useful state. I also removed the separate readout box where it duplicated the in-scene explanation. I retained the settings, visible geometry and reset action because removing those would make the experiment harder to interpret. My aim was to reduce the work of operating the page while keeping the information needed to reason about the model.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-26\">What I want this to achieve<\/h3><p>Each removal was intended to reduce competition around useful information. I retained visible settings, the experiment itself and reset controls because these help people interpret and recover from an action. Simplicity should remove friction without removing necessary explanation.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"criterion-7\"><summary>07 Progressive disclosure<\/summary><div><h3 id=\"nav-section-27\">Why it matters to me<\/h3><p>I make essential information available immediately and place supporting detail where people can choose to open it. This accommodates different intentions and levels of interest without making every visit equally demanding.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-28\">How I applied it<\/h3><p>I made the design rationale easy to discover at the opening without requiring visitors to read it before trying an activity. The entry choices each carry a short description; the detailed reasoning sits behind the selected route. Within the project, teaching pathways and supporting design explanations use expandable sections. I applied a different rule to information that affects interpretation: the invented nature of the snap remains beside the animation. This distinction prevents progressive disclosure from becoming an excuse to hide an essential qualification. The visitor chooses the depth of the account, while the interface still supplies what is needed for an informed action.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-29\">What I want this to achieve<\/h3><p>This approach keeps the main experience focused while allowing professional scrutiny. I keep instructions and the limitation of the mock snap close to their point of use, because essential information should not depend on discovering an optional disclosure.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"criterion-8\"><summary>08 Plain precise language<\/summary><div><h3 id=\"nav-section-30\">Why it matters to me<\/h3><p>I choose wording that helps people understand an action or concept with as little interpretation as possible. Brevity is valuable when it preserves meaning; a shorter phrase is not automatically clearer.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-31\">How I applied it<\/h3><p>I tested the meaning of short labels against the action they needed to communicate. The margin wording moved from more in this direction to more here and finally Scroll to explore: the final phrase identifies an action rather than simply pointing at unspecified content. For section 06, I made the opposite choice and retained Instructional design and user interface considerations instead of the shorter Design deep dive. The longer title names the professional subject an employer may be looking for. In both cases I chose specificity over a rule that every label should be as short as possible, and allowed the menu title to wrap rather than removing its meaning.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-32\">What I want this to achieve<\/h3><p>These decisions use language to set expectations. The short cue supports scanning, while the explicit section title helps visitors decide whether to open it. I would check comprehension with visitors rather than judging clarity from word count alone.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"criterion-9\"><summary>09 Visual hierarchy and attention<\/summary><div><h3 id=\"nav-section-33\">Why it matters to me<\/h3><p>I use layout, typography, spacing and emphasis to show what belongs together and what deserves attention first. A consistent hierarchy makes a page easier to scan and reduces the need to interpret every component separately.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-34\">How I applied it<\/h3><p>I worked on the relationship between controls as well as their individual appearance. Comparable actions were aligned along their bottom edges so differences in paragraph length did not leave the buttons scattered. I reduced the language and utility controls to make room for breadcrumbs in the same fixed-header row, then aligned the breadcrumb text with the language-button text and the left edge of the body. I also changed the active-language fill from black to dark green and brought stray blue links into the Education palette. These decisions give hierarchy a repeatable structure instead of relying on a separate treatment for every component.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-35\">What I want this to achieve<\/h3><p>These choices create a more deliberate relationship between content and controls. I balance compactness with legibility and usable targets; the layout still needs checking with enlarged text, wrapping labels and narrow viewports.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"criterion-10\"><summary>10 Meaningful use of media<\/summary><div><h3 id=\"nav-section-36\">Why it matters to me<\/h3><p>I give media a defined function. An image, animation or spoken explanation should orient, demonstrate, clarify or provide an alternative way to access content. Media that competes with the task can increase effort even when it is visually appealing.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-37\">How I applied it<\/h3><p>I assigned the avatar a bounded task: explain the current page and help the visitor begin. I used page-specific recorded introductions rather than reading the entire page by default, and kept the guide in a consistent position with transparent artwork. I made it fade after speaking and return when an introduction is requested. That required attention to the layout as well as the portrait: the guide must not leave a permanent gap or push later-page content down unnecessarily. I refined the mouth movement, head movement and background treatment because an unconvincing talking figure can distract from the explanation it is intended to support.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-38\">What I want this to achieve<\/h3><p>The avatar is intended to explain the page and help visitors begin. It should support the written experience and remain under user control. I retained written alternatives and reduced-motion handling; full narration of this report will follow content approval.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"criterion-11\"><summary>11 Examples and demonstration<\/summary><div><h3 id=\"nav-section-39\">Why it matters to me<\/h3><p>I use examples to make an explanation observable. A demonstration must represent the relationship being described accurately enough for its purpose; otherwise it can reinforce the wrong understanding.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-40\">How I applied it<\/h3><p>I checked whether each visible change actually represented the setting being altered. A span slider is difficult to interpret if the supports remain fixed, so I made their positions change with span. A diameter control is undermined if the stick disappears at a larger value, so I corrected the rendering across that range and kept the wood-like form legible. I also distinguished two kinds of behaviour: the elastic bending model and the deliberately invented break event. This keeps the demonstration inspectable. A visitor should be able to connect the value, the changed geometry and the explanation, rather than accept the animation because it looks plausible.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-41\">What I want this to achieve<\/h3><p>The representation connects a control to its physical meaning in the illustration. I distinguish the elastic model from the invented snap trigger and check the full control range, because a convincing appearance must not conceal a misleading or broken relationship.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"criterion-12\"><summary>12 Meaningful participation<\/summary><div><h3 id=\"nav-section-42\">Why it matters to me<\/h3><p>I design interaction around a useful choice and its consequence. Clicking is an input method; the design value lies in the prediction, comparison, investigation or decision it enables.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-43\">How I applied it<\/h3><p>I built the interaction around prediction, manipulation and observation. Visitors can alter the model settings, run the experiment and restore a known starting point with Reset. I moved Run and Reset inside the animation window before Try the snap, aligning them as one action group. That places the deliberate experiment before the dramatic shortcut and connects the controls with the scene they affect. The remaining design challenge is to make the reasoning as compelling as the action: prompts to change one variable and explain a result are important because operating the model successfully does not, on its own, demonstrate understanding.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-44\">What I want this to achieve<\/h3><p>Grouping actions with the scene connects an input to its visible result. To strengthen the investigation, I would ask visitors to vary one factor, explain the observation and test another case. That provides a more useful outcome than repeated activation of the snap shortcut.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"criterion-13\"><summary>13 Feedback and visible status<\/summary><div><h3 id=\"nav-section-45\">Why it matters to me<\/h3><p>I make the consequences of an action understandable. Useful feedback helps people recognise an available action, confirm a change and decide what to do next. Its meaning matters more than the amount of feedback.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-46\">How I applied it<\/h3><p>I gave different events different feedback rather than treating every response as interchangeable. Links and buttons have a shared hover treatment and an audible activation click. The experiment changes visibly when it runs and uses a cracking sound for the illustrative snap. The scroll arrows are an explicit exception: their ratchet-like sound accompanies movement instead of adding the ordinary click. I removed the passive Ready to test badge because it added a signal without helping the visitor interpret an action. I also recognise the gap in the current system: avatar mute does not control these interface sounds, so a global sound preference is still needed.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-47\">What I want this to achieve<\/h3><p>Different feedback serves different purposes: hover signals interactivity, a click confirms activation, and the changing scene illustrates an outcome. Sound supplements visible feedback. A global sound preference remains an important improvement, since avatar mute does not silence every interface sound.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"criterion-14\"><summary>14 User control and pacing<\/summary><div><h3 id=\"nav-section-48\">Why it matters to me<\/h3><p>I allow people to manage pace, revisit information and control optional media. This supports different reading speeds and circumstances and reduces the risk that the interface takes attention away from the visitor’s chosen task.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-49\">How I applied it<\/h3><p>I placed control beside the media it affects. The avatar’s mute control appears beneath it while narration is running, rather than occupying the header permanently. The introduction can be requested again, and the avatar returns for it. I also made the space reserved for the guide collapse after speech, so visitors regain reading space without a sudden layout jump. These changes address both pacing and attention, but I do not treat mute as a substitute for stopping speech or reducing motion. A complete control model needs to distinguish those behaviours, and the transition must be checked to ensure it does not disturb someone already reading.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-50\">What I want this to achieve<\/h3><p>Contextual controls place the action beside the media it affects. I distinguish mute from pause, stop and motion control: they serve different needs. I also need to verify that animated layout changes preserve reading position and respect reduced-motion preferences.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"criterion-15\"><summary>15 Consistency and predictability<\/summary><div><h3 id=\"nav-section-51\">Why it matters to me<\/h3><p>I establish repeatable conventions so people can apply what they have already learned elsewhere in the experience. Consistency reduces relearning and creates a dependable basis for future additions.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-52\">How I applied it<\/h3><p>I converted repeated corrections into shared rules rather than leaving them as isolated page fixes. The same hover, focus, activation and alignment behaviour applies to navigation, ordinary links, disclosures and return links. The Education colour rules extend to active states and subordinate pages, so imported defaults do not introduce unrelated blue, purple or black treatments. I recorded those choices as standards for future projects, with each section using its own coordinated palette. This gives new components a starting point and makes exceptions deliberate: the scroll arrows retain the shared visual language while using feedback suited to continuous movement.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-53\">What I want this to achieve<\/h3><p>I recorded these choices as portfolio standards, with a coordinated palette for each section. Exceptions should have a reason: the scrolling arrows use a movement sound rather than the ordinary click because their feedback corresponds to continued movement.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"criterion-16\"><summary>16 Navigation and orientation<\/summary><div><h3 id=\"nav-section-54\">Why it matters to me<\/h3><p>I help people understand where they are, what is available and how to return. Navigation between pages and movement within a page are different tasks; each needs a clear, predictable control.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-55\">How I applied it<\/h3><p>I chose to keep breadcrumbs in the fixed header because visitors need a reliable route back while exploring long activity pages. This created competition for space with the language controls, so I reduced those controls and aligned the breadcrumb text with them while retaining alignment to the body. I kept the numbered menu for movement between project sections and introduced conditional triangles for movement within a page. The upper arrow appears when content exists above; the lower one appears when content exists below. Their positions and label remain fixed when one arrow disappears, so the navigation aid does not shift as the visitor reaches a boundary.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-56\">What I want this to achieve<\/h3><p>Breadcrumbs provide location and return paths; the triangles provide page movement. Fixed arrow positions keep the cue stable when one arrow disappears. Accessible names, keyboard activation and sufficient clearance from body text remain necessary checks, especially on mobile.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"criterion-17\"><summary>17 Error prevention and recovery<\/summary><div><h3 id=\"nav-section-57\">Why it matters to me<\/h3><p>I make exploration recoverable and prevent avoidable failures. People should understand how to restore a useful state, and the design should fail in a way that preserves meaning rather than silently removing it.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-58\">How I applied it<\/h3><p>I provided Reset as a visible recovery action within the experiment, beside Run, so testing a different setting does not require reloading the page. I also used a navigation failure to examine the shared implementation: section 06 showed a number but no title because the language updater did not recognise the new key. I added the translated label and a fallback that retains meaningful text. The important correction was to the behaviour that could affect future additions, rather than merely forcing one title to appear. This is why I would include language switching and recovery paths in checks after changes to shared components.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-59\">What I want this to achieve<\/h3><p>Reset encourages exploration without requiring a page reload. The menu correction addresses a shared-system weakness rather than hiding the symptom. I would check each supported language after navigation changes and verify that reset restores both the controls and the visible model.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"criterion-18\"><summary>18 Accessibility and inclusive alternatives<\/summary><div><h3 id=\"nav-section-60\">Why it matters to me<\/h3><p>I consider whether people can perceive, understand and operate the experience under different conditions. Accessibility includes language, hearing, vision, movement, input method and the environment in which someone is using the design.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-61\">How I applied it<\/h3><p>I built alternatives into the presentation: visible English, Spanish and Chinese choices, written explanations and transcripts alongside optional speech, and visible feedback alongside sound. I applied keyboard-focus feedback and reduced-motion handling in the shared interface. I also treated language as part of navigation reliability, correcting the missing label when a new menu item met the translation system. These are concrete provisions, with clear limits: some body translation is incomplete, the rotated scroll cue needs usable control labels and target sizes, and a global sound preference is absent. I would test the whole journey with assistive technology and different settings before claiming accessibility conformance.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-62\">What I want this to achieve<\/h3><p>These features provide alternatives, but they do not establish conformance. Body translation remains incomplete in parts of the project. My next checks include keyboard order, contrast, zoom, screen-reader labels, target sizes, motion and a global sound preference.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"criterion-19\"><summary>19 Appropriate challenge and support<\/summary><div><h3 id=\"nav-section-63\">Why it matters to me<\/h3><p>I aim for a level of challenge that serves the intended outcome, with support available when it is needed. Too little challenge can make participation superficial; too much can prevent people from reaching the central idea.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-64\">How I applied it<\/h3><p>I used a common investigation to make the difference in challenge visible. The school pathway builds around observation, prediction and a fair test; the university pathway asks for modelling, analysis, uncertainty and a more defensible conclusion. I provided supporting materials and tutor perspectives so independence does not mean leaving the learner without a route to help. The design task is to vary the demand and support coherently, rather than make one version longer or more technical. I would check that balance by observing what each group can explain independently and where prompts or examples are needed.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-65\">What I want this to achieve<\/h3><p>I want people to engage with the reasoning at an appropriate level of independence. I would observe where each group hesitates or needs help, then adjust prompts, examples and support. Audience labels alone cannot demonstrate that the challenge is well matched.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"criterion-20\"><summary>20 Testing and iterative improvement<\/summary><div><h3 id=\"nav-section-66\">Why it matters to me<\/h3><p>I can become very good at using something I have built—and miss how difficult it is for someone seeing it for the first time. That is why I keep asking whether my assumptions are correct. Testing helps me find the successes worth protecting as well as the sticking points I need to fix. Experience helps me choose what to try; feedback tells me where to look again.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-67\">How I applied it<\/h3><p>I revised the project in response to identifiable failures rather than accepting the first working version. Screenshot reviews exposed misplaced breadcrumbs, excessive control height, avatar-induced layout gaps, unwanted outlines, a disappearing stick and a blank navigation title. I connected each observation to a specific change, and preserved selected earlier screenshots in this account so the reasoning can be inspected. That provides evidence of iteration, not evidence of independent usability or learning effectiveness. The next step is to move from owner review to observed tasks with representative users and feedback from tutors and institutional stakeholders, then judge revisions against agreed outcomes.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-68\">What I want this to achieve<\/h3><p>These reviews identified concrete defects and informed corrections. They are formative owner reviews, not independent usability tests or proof of improved understanding. I would now observe representative visitors completing defined tasks and use their performance to prioritise the next changes.<\/p><\/div><\/details><\/div><section id=\"graphic-design\"><h2 id=\"nav-section-69\">Graphic design that earns its place<\/h2><p>How a screen looks affects what people notice, how confidently they act and whether they want to stay with it. I therefore consider the visual design alongside the instructions and interaction. The question is not simply whether it looks attractive; it is what the visual choices help someone understand or do.<\/p><p>The following twenty-four considerations come from the supplied <em>Graphic Design Considerations for Computer Screens<\/em> checklist. It is a practical synthesis, not a single published standard. There is deliberate overlap with the twenty broader criteria: here I look more closely at what happens on the screen.<\/p><p>You can scan the headings below for the points that interest you. Select a heading or its arrow to open the design question and see how I applied it in this project; select it again to close it. Open as many as you like, in any order. This lets you explore a particular decision without reading every consideration.<\/p><div class=\"graphic-index-columns\"><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"graphic-1\"><summary>01 Purpose<\/summary><div><p><strong>The question.<\/strong> What should this screen help someone understand or do? Does its visual design support that purpose?<\/p><p><strong>In this project.<\/strong> I ask whether each screen makes its next useful action clear. The opening now offers a brief choice between examining my design thinking and exploring the courses, with the detailed account behind the chosen route.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"graphic-2\"><summary>02 Audience<\/summary><div><p><strong>The question.<\/strong> Are the visual choices appropriate for the users’ age, experience, expectations and viewing needs?<\/p><p><strong>In this project.<\/strong> The school and university routes need different levels of explanation. I also consider the employer scanning the portfolio: a clear opening, descriptive headings and direct routes to the rationale help that visitor decide what to inspect.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"graphic-3\"><summary>03 Visual hierarchy<\/summary><div><p><strong>The question.<\/strong> What should people notice first, second and third? Do size, position and emphasis make that order clear?<\/p><p><strong>In this project.<\/strong> I use distinct heading and body treatments and keep the primary entry choices prominent. The test is whether a new visitor notices the intended starting points, rather than whichever component happens to be largest or most animated.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"graphic-4\"><summary>04 Layout and composition<\/summary><div><p><strong>The question.<\/strong> Are the elements arranged in a clear, balanced way? Does the screen feel organised?<\/p><p><strong>In this project.<\/strong> I keep the main reading area, fixed navigation and page-movement controls in recognisable positions. The composition still needs checking at narrow widths, where the inset arrows could compete for the same space as content.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"graphic-5\"><summary>05 Alignment<\/summary><div><p><strong>The question.<\/strong> Do text, images and controls follow consistent alignment lines?<\/p><p><strong>In this project.<\/strong> I aligned breadcrumb text with the body and the language-control text, and aligned comparable card actions along their bottoms. Consistent alignment makes related choices easier to compare when descriptions have different lengths.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"graphic-6\"><summary>06 Grouping and proximity<\/summary><div><p><strong>The question.<\/strong> Are related elements visibly grouped together, with enough separation from unrelated content?<\/p><p><strong>In this project.<\/strong> I placed Run, Reset and Try the snap together inside the animation window. The controls now belong visually to the scene they change, rather than appearing as separate actions elsewhere on the page.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"graphic-7\"><summary>07 White space<\/summary><div><p><strong>The question.<\/strong> Is there enough empty space to separate information, support reading and avoid crowding?<\/p><p><strong>In this project.<\/strong> I removed the unnecessary space left by the avatar after speech while retaining separation around text and controls. Empty space should support reading and grouping; it should not make the visitor scroll past an unexplained gap.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"graphic-8\"><summary>08 Information density<\/summary><div><p><strong>The question.<\/strong> How much is visible at once? Can users find what matters without feeling overwhelmed?<\/p><p><strong>In this project.<\/strong> I reduced oversized buttons and removed duplicate messages. I keep the opening choices short and place detailed explanations in their destinations, so visitors can decide how much of the account they want to read.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"graphic-9\"><summary>09 Typography<\/summary><div><p><strong>The question.<\/strong> Are the typefaces, sizes, weights and line spacing readable and appropriate? Are headings clearly different from body text?<\/p><p><strong>In this project.<\/strong> I use a serif heading style with a simpler body and control typeface to distinguish roles. I would check the smallest header text and wrapped menu labels with enlarged text before treating the current sizing as settled.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"graphic-10\"><summary>10 Text presentation<\/summary><div><p><strong>The question.<\/strong> Are line lengths comfortable? Are paragraphs, labels and alignment easy to scan and read?<\/p><p><strong>In this project.<\/strong> I break the rationale into named criteria with a clickable index and return links. Paragraphs explain a decision in connected language; headings let a visitor find one point without reading the entire report.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"graphic-11\"><summary>11 Colour palette<\/summary><div><p><strong>The question.<\/strong> Do the colours work together, suit the intended character and support a coherent appearance?<\/p><p><strong>In this project.<\/strong> Education uses coordinated cream, sage and dark green across backgrounds, links, controls and subordinate pages. Other portfolio sections should have their own related palette, rather than inherit Education colours indiscriminately.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"graphic-12\"><summary>12 Contrast<\/summary><div><p><strong>The question.<\/strong> Can users distinguish text, controls and important details from their backgrounds?<\/p><p><strong>In this project.<\/strong> Text and controls need to remain distinguishable against the muted backgrounds. The palette establishes the direction; measured contrast checks across default, hover, active and focus states are still required.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"graphic-13\"><summary>13 Meaning of colour<\/summary><div><p><strong>The question.<\/strong> Is colour used consistently? Is meaning also communicated through words, symbols or shapes?<\/p><p><strong>In this project.<\/strong> I pair colour with other signals. The selected language has a labelled control, the scroll arrows have a direction and text cue, and the experiment shows a changed scene as well as playing sound. Colour alone should not carry the essential meaning.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"graphic-14\"><summary>14 Images and illustration<\/summary><div><p><strong>The question.<\/strong> Do visuals explain, orient or add useful character? Are they clear, relevant and appropriately sized?<\/p><p><strong>In this project.<\/strong> The stick illustration connects the values to a recognisable object, and the transparent avatar has an orienting role. I corrected the missing stick at larger diameters because a decorative finish cannot compensate for a demonstration that disappears.<\/p><\/div><span class=\"illustration-plan-marker\" id=\"illustration-40\" aria-hidden=\"true\"><\/span><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"graphic-15\"><summary>15 Icons and symbols<\/summary><div><p><strong>The question.<\/strong> Will the audience understand them? Do unfamiliar or ambiguous icons need text labels?<\/p><p><strong>In this project.<\/strong> I use simple up and down triangles with the label Scroll to explore. The label helps explain the purpose, while the controls have accessible names. I would check whether visitors recognise that the triangles themselves can be activated.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"graphic-16\"><summary>16 Consistency<\/summary><div><p><strong>The question.<\/strong> Do similar elements look similar across screens? Are fonts, spacing, colours and shapes applied predictably?<\/p><p><strong>In this project.<\/strong> I apply shared control shapes, section colours, hover behaviour and alignment across the pages. A newly added menu item also has to survive the language updater; consistency includes reliable behaviour as well as appearance.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"graphic-17\"><summary>17 Recognisable controls<\/summary><div><p><strong>The question.<\/strong> Is it obvious what can be clicked or selected? Are controls visually distinguishable from decoration?<\/p><p><strong>In this project.<\/strong> I removed the Ready to test badge because its control-like appearance invited an action it did not provide. Links, buttons and expandable summaries need recognisable affordances and useful responses.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"graphic-18\"><summary>18 Visual feedback<\/summary><div><p><strong>The question.<\/strong> Are selected, loading, completed, disabled and error states clearly represented?<\/p><p><strong>In this project.<\/strong> The triangles fill dark green during activation, ordinary controls have hover feedback, and the model shows its changed geometry. The next review should check that keyboard and touch users can identify the relevant states too.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"graphic-19\"><summary>19 Motion<\/summary><div><p><strong>The question.<\/strong> Does animation help explain a change or guide attention? Can distracting or uncomfortable movement be reduced?<\/p><p><strong>In this project.<\/strong> I use movement to explain the model and a speaking avatar, then reduce competition when the explanation ends. Reduced-motion handling and animated layout changes need checking together, including whether reading position remains stable.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"graphic-20\"><summary>20 Screen size and scaling<\/summary><div><p><strong>The question.<\/strong> Does the composition remain usable on different displays, at higher zoom levels and with enlarged text?<\/p><p><strong>In this project.<\/strong> I allow navigation and content to reflow, with a mobile menu for smaller screens. The long section title, fixed header and inset scroll controls make zoom and narrow-screen checks particularly important.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"graphic-21\"><summary>21 Accessibility<\/summary><div><p><strong>The question.<\/strong> Can people with different visual, motor or cognitive needs perceive and use the design?<\/p><p><strong>In this project.<\/strong> I consider focus visibility, readable labels, text alternatives, language choice and optional media together. These provisions need whole-journey testing with different inputs and assistive technology; they are not a substitute for an accessibility review.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"graphic-22\"><summary>22 Emotional response<\/summary><div><p><strong>The question.<\/strong> Does the screen feel inviting, trustworthy and appropriate? Does its appearance encourage engagement?<\/p><p><strong>In this project.<\/strong> I want the experience to feel welcoming and worth exploring. The familiar material, restrained palette and responsive model are ways of exploring that response. I would ask what feels inviting or irritating and observe how people actually use it.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"graphic-23\"><summary>23 Visual restraint<\/summary><div><p><strong>The question.<\/strong> Does each decorative element contribute something useful, or compete with the main content?<\/p><p><strong>In this project.<\/strong> I removed the avatar outline, unwanted surrounds on the triangles and redundant status information. I ask what each detail contributes before retaining it. An element can add character, but it should not compete with an instruction or result.<\/p><\/div><\/details><details class=\"graphic-consideration\" id=\"graphic-24\"><summary>24 Testing and refinement<\/summary><div><p><strong>The question.<\/strong> Do users notice, understand and respond as expected? What needs changing after observing them use it?<\/p><p><strong>In this project.<\/strong> I use screenshot reviews to identify specific defects, then change the component responsible. Representative-user observation and feedback after real use would be the next sources of evidence; those have not yet been collected for this sketch.<\/p><\/div><\/details><\/div><a class=\"report-back\" href=\"#report-index\">Back to index ↑<\/a><\/section><section id=\"ai-development\"><h2 id=\"nav-section-70\">Using AI to build the web experience<\/h2><p>I am not a coder, so AI has been the practical way for me to build the web component of this project. It has also become a useful learning opportunity: I can turn an idea into something I can explore, question and improve. For me personally, that is a fantastic tool. It supports a non-linear approach to development, allowing me to move between the overall experience and the details, try alternatives and revisit earlier decisions as the project takes shape.<\/p><p>What it does not bring is my understanding of the purpose, the audience or the standards I want the experience to meet. It can generate a plausible solution without fully recognising why that solution is wrong for this setting. I cannot rely on it to share my intentions or exercise the judgement I have developed through experience. I have to make the brief clear, explain the criteria that matter and examine what it actually produces.<\/p><p>That has been very visible in this project. I have used AI to help build the pages, navigation and interactions, then reviewed the results and asked for specific revisions: making important choices easier to find, replacing long linked lists with expandable headings, giving opened explanations the full page width and removing sections that did not earn their place. Each change starts with a judgement about what someone needs from the experience. AI helps me implement and explore that judgement; I remain responsible for deciding whether the result serves its purpose.<\/p><p>There is a technical boundary here too. Knowing what I want an interface to do is not the same as being able to verify every line of code behind it. I can examine its behaviour, check it against the design criteria and test realistic tasks, but a production commission may also need a developer to review areas beyond my expertise, including security, maintainability and deployment. A page that looks finished is not, by itself, evidence that all of those requirements have been met.<\/p><p>My view is that AI makes expertise more useful by giving it another way to act. It does not remove the need for that expertise. Without a good grasp of the subject, it is easy to accept something convincing that misses the point. Getting to an acceptable, polished result takes informed decisions, clear feedback and repeated examination of the output. My mantra applies here as much as anywhere else: test, test, test. AI helps me move the work forward; I still have to decide what good looks like and gather evidence that we are getting there.<\/p><\/section><section id=\"design-evaluation\"><h2 id=\"nav-section-71\">Test the assumptions, then improve the experience<\/h2><p>This sketch shows how I frame a problem, develop an experience and refine the details. It makes my decisions visible, but the real test is what happens when people use it. Can they understand the instructions, find what they need and complete the intended activities? Where do they hesitate, ask for help or interpret something differently from what I expected? I would also want to know how the experience feels: whether it invites curiosity, builds confidence and makes people want to continue.<\/p><p>A live commission would bring learners, tutors, administrators and other stakeholders into that process. Together, we would confirm the need, agree what success looks like and establish the practical constraints, including time, access, available support and the delivery setting. I would then observe representative users attempting realistic tasks, listen to their feedback and review evidence of understanding and performance. That would help distinguish an interface problem from an unclear instruction, a gap in prior knowledge or an activity that needs a different approach.<\/p><p>The aim would be to turn those findings into specific improvements, then test again to see whether the changes helped. I would prioritise barriers that prevent participation or understanding, protect the parts that work well and continue gathering feedback after release. Those people, constraints and findings cannot be invented for this demonstration. They are the next stage of the work, where my assumptions would be challenged by experience in use.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-72\">Put it in front of people who have not helped build it<\/h3><p>The screenshot reviews caught real problems: a missing stick, misplaced breadcrumbs, unwanted outlines and a blank menu label. They helped improve the implementation. They do not tell me whether an unfamiliar learner can navigate confidently or explain what the model represents.<\/p><p>I would observe representatives of both student groups completing short tasks without coaching: find an activity, predict a result, change one variable, explain the observation and recover using Reset. I would record wrong turns, requests for help and explanations, as well as task completion. I would then revise and repeat. Enjoying the snap, operating the controls and understanding the investigation are different outcomes.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-73\">Listen to the people who have to deliver it<\/h3><p>Learners are central, but they are not the only users. Tutors need to judge whether instructions, assessment prompts and evidence are useful in practice. I would ask them to walk through preparation, delivery, feedback and follow-up, identifying where they would have to improvise or do extra work.<\/p><p>I would also seek feedback from the relevant programme lead, accessibility and learning-support colleagues, and technical or administrative teams. Their priorities may conflict: more reporting can help oversight while increasing workload; extra guidance can help one group while slowing another. I would make those trade-offs visible and agree priorities with the people responsible for the outcome.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-74\">Find out what the institution actually needs<\/h3><p>No institutional fit has been established for this fictional brief. Before recommending adoption, I would clarify the curriculum and assessment requirements, delivery model, technology environment, learner support arrangements and ownership of updates. I would also establish what progress information is genuinely required, who needs access and how it should be handled.<\/p><p>A start-to-finish package must fit the way people work. That could mean revising the assessment, changing a tutor view, simplifying data collection or adapting the resources for an existing learning platform. The prototype gives us something concrete to discuss; it does not settle those decisions in advance.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-75\">Keep the attractive parts honest<\/h3><p>The <a href=\"learning-school-activity.html#nav-section-1\" onclick=\"sessionStorage.setItem('jp-open-snap-demo','1')\">snap is a deliberately invented extreme-setting event<\/a>, not a calculation of real breaking strength. The language options demonstrate an inclusive direction, but body translation remains incomplete in parts of the project. Audio and motion provide additional ways to engage, but they need effective control and cannot carry essential information alone.<\/p><p>My next practical checks would cover keyboard use, screen-reader labels, contrast, enlarged text, reduced motion and mobile spacing around the inset arrows. I would complete language coverage and introduce a global sound preference. Full-report narration will follow once the wording is settled. I would make accessibility claims only against a defined review, not from the presence of individual features.<\/p><h3 id=\"nav-section-76\">Agree what success looks like<\/h3><p>I would agree success criteria before a pilot: what visitors should find, what learners should be able to explain or apply, what tutors should be able to deliver and what information the institution needs. Measures should follow those questions. A polished interface is one part of the evidence, not the outcome itself.<\/p><p>That is the approach I want this project to demonstrate: I connect the detail of an experience to its purpose, make my reasoning available for scrutiny and use feedback to decide what to improve. The sketch starts the conversation. I want users and stakeholders to help me find what I have missed. A working solution develops through that exchange, supported by evidence and a clear understanding of the setting.<\/p><a class=\"report-back\" href=\"#report-index\">Back to index ↑<\/a><\/section><section aria-labelledby=\"audience-interface-design\"><h2 id=\"audience-interface-design\">Two audiences, two interface approaches<\/h2><p>The age-15 route presents the investigation as a challenge: illustrated stick choices make differences visible, short instructions such as “Can you outsmart a stick?” invite action, and the animated stick guide offers help beside the task. Keeping the selected stick consistent in the bending lab and answer prompts reduces the need to remember earlier choices. The undergraduate route gives more prominence to quantities, units, tables and model assumptions, using technical language and asking learners to interpret evidence with greater independence. I selected three areas for comparison: choosing a stick, operating the model and explaining a result. In each, the younger route makes the next step more explicit, while the undergraduate route expects a more analytical response. Both retain consistent navigation, language choices, readable controls and the option to control voice and motion. These are design decisions to test with learners, rather than assumptions that everyone of one age needs the same interface.<\/p><span class=\"illustration-plan-marker\" id=\"illustration-41\" aria-hidden=\"true\"><\/span><p><a class=\"project-index-link\" href=\"learning-school-activity.html#nav-section-1\">15 year old lesson<\/a> · <a class=\"project-index-link\" href=\"learning-university-activity.html#nav-section-1\">Undergraduate lesson<\/a><\/p><\/section><span id=\"illustration-38\" aria-hidden=\"true\"><\/span><section id=\"diverse-avatar-guides\"><h2 id=\"diverse-avatar-heading\">Diverse guides and representation<\/h2><p>I introduced eight adult guides, aged 30–60, with varied appearances and contemporary clothing, so that the interface presents expertise through a broader range of people. Sofía is a fictional Spanish guide, aged 46, shown in Teaching materials and Interactive demos. Yusuf and Elena extend the cast with Middle Eastern and Mexican character designs. These are individual fictional people, not templates for entire communities. Guides were allocated across sections and their assignments remain fixed to preserve familiarity. Each guide follows the selected English, Spanish or Mandarin introduction; appearance does not determine language or accent. style=\"grid-column:1/-1\" hidden><\/section><main class=\"shell report\" id=\"mainContent\"><section id=\"ai-development\"><h2 id=\"nav-section-1\">Using AI to build the web experience<\/h2><p>I am not a coder, so AI has been the practical way for me to build the web component of this project. It has also become a useful learning opportunity: I can turn an idea into something I can explore, question and improve. For me personally, that is a fantastic tool. It supports a non-linear approach to development, allowing me to move between the overall experience and the details, try alternatives and revisit earlier decisions as the project takes shape.<\/p><p>What it does not bring is my understanding of the purpose, the audience or the standards I want the experience to meet. It can generate a plausible solution without fully recognising why that solution is wrong for this setting. I cannot rely on it to share my intentions or exercise the judgement I have developed through experience. I have to make the brief clear, explain the criteria that matter and examine what it actually produces.<\/p><p>That has been very visible in this project. I have used AI to help build the pages, navigation and interactions, then reviewed the results and asked for specific revisions: making important choices easier to find, replacing long linked lists with expandable headings, giving opened explanations the full page width and removing sections that did not earn their place. Each change starts with a judgement about what someone needs from the experience. AI helps me implement and explore that judgement; I remain responsible for deciding whether the result serves its purpose.<\/p><p>There is a technical boundary here too. Knowing what I want an interface to do is not the same as being able to verify every line of code behind it. I can examine its behaviour, check it against the design criteria and test realistic tasks, but a production commission may also need a developer to review areas beyond my expertise, including security, maintainability and deployment. A page that looks finished is not, by itself, evidence that all of those requirements have been met.<\/p><p>My view is that AI makes expertise more useful by giving it another way to act. It does not remove the need for that expertise. Without a good grasp of the subject, it is easy to accept something convincing that misses the point. Getting to an acceptable, polished result takes informed decisions, clear feedback and repeated examination of the output. My mantra applies here as much as anywhere else: test, test, test. AI helps me move the work forward; I still have to decide what good looks like and gather evidence that we are getting there.<\/p><\/section><span id=\"illustration-42\" aria-hidden=\"true\"><\/span><\/main>\n<section class=\"card\" id=\"designExplanation\" style=\"grid-column:1/-1\"><\/section><footer>Jonathan Pincher · <a href=\"education.html\">Back to Education &amp; Learning Design<\/a><\/footer><\/div><script>\n(()=>{\nif(location.hostname==='jpincher.github.io'){const online=document.getElementById('onlineAccess');if(online)online.hidden=true;}const $=id=>document.getElementById(id),lang=$('guideLanguage');let saved='en';try{saved=localStorage.getItem('jp-guide-language')||'en'}catch{}if(!['en','es','zh'].includes(saved))saved='en';lang.value=saved;\nconst copy={en:{heading:'Your section guide',play:'Play introduction',stop:'Stop',note:'Navigation and introductions are available in three languages. Calcule la media de las lecturas válidas y represente diámetro en el eje horizontal y desplazamiento medio en el vertical, con unidades y escalas regulares. No una los puntos por orden de muestra ni elimine un resultado solo porque contradice la predicción. Si el tiempo no basta, reduzca el número de muestras o separe la sesión de gráficos tras probar la carga de trabajo.<\/p><h3>Clase 4 · Evaluar y aplicar · 60 minutos<\/h3><p>Determine si las pruebas apoyan la hipótesis. Cite al menos dos resultados, explique dos limitaciones y una mejora relacionada para cada una. Recomiende muestras para miembros de un pequeño puente de maqueta con una luz indicada por el docente. Incluya un boceto y nuevas pruebas necesarias: uniones, configuración, cargas repetidas y resistencia a la rotura. La recomendación no demuestra capacidad de carga ni seguridad del puente.<\/p><h3>Hojas de trabajo esenciales<\/h3><p>Registro: muestra; longitud; diámetro; masa; textura; estado; observaciones. Plan: pregunta; hipótesis; variable comparada; resultado medido; controles; método; factores no controlados; condiciones de parada; aprobación. Resultados: muestra; diámetro en mm; desplazamientos 1, 2 y 3 en mm; media. Registre también luz, carga total y tiempo de lectura.<\/p><p>Media = suma de desplazamientos válidos ÷ número de lecturas válidas. Ejemplo simulado: (4 + 5 + 3) ÷ 3 = 4 mm. No copie datos simulados como resultados experimentales. Una menor flexión en condiciones equivalentes indica mayor resistencia a la flexión en ese montaje, no mayor carga de rotura.<\/p><h3>Actividades de razonamiento<\/h3><p>Clasifique observaciones, inferencias y predicciones. Ejemplos: «la balanza indica 24 g» es una observación; «puede contener más humedad» es una inferencia; «con la misma carga se doblará menos» es una predicción. Audite un plan que usa distinta carga y separación entre apoyos para palos gruesos y finos. Corrija controles, lecturas, muestreo y la conclusión errónea de que el que menos se dobla es siempre el más resistente.<\/p><h3>Evaluación y respuestas<\/h3><p>Producto final individual: pregunta e hipótesis, método y variables, tabla y gráfico, conclusión con resultados, dos limitaciones y mejoras, y recomendación justificada. Puede utilizar datos de grupo, pero la explicación debe ser individual; una presentación grabada equivalente conserva las mismas exigencias.<\/p><p>Prueba separada de 10 puntos: resultado medido y unidad, 2; dos controles, 2; media de 3, 4 y 5 mm, 1; diferencia entre repetición y muestras independientes, 2; diferencia entre flexión y rotura, 1; limitación y mejora relacionada, 2. Respuestas: desplazamiento vertical del punto medio en mm; controles como luz y carga; media de 4 mm; las repeticiones informan de consistencia, las muestras independientes de variación entre muestras; no se midió la carga de rotura.<\/p><p>Rúbrica de investigación: cinco criterios, de 0 a 3 puntos cada uno, total 15: observación y medición; planificación; análisis; conclusión y aplicación; evaluación. 0: sin evidencia pertinente. 1: evidencia parcial o inconsistente. 2: evidencia clara y mayoritariamente correcta. 3: evidencia precisa, justificada y con límites explícitos, según los descriptores originales. Informe los 15 puntos y la prueba de 10 por separado; no son límites de calificación GCSE validados.<\/p><h3>Apoyo, IA y evaluación de la enseñanza<\/h3><p>Use vocabulario visual, ejemplos, tablas guiadas, escalas sugeridas y respuestas orales cuando proceda. Amplíe mediante resolución instrumental, variación y diseños que controlen factores de confusión. La IA manejada por el docente puede ayudar a redactar recursos y ejemplos deliberadamente erróneos, siempre revisados y etiquetados; no se requieren cuentas del alumnado. Compruebe afirmaciones científicas y no suba trabajos identificables. Tras impartir, revise respuestas iniciales y finales, trabajos, participación, tiempos y accesibilidad. No se han medido aún resultados de aprendizaje ni ahorro de tiempo.<\/p>\", \"university\": \"<h2>Guía docente en español: primer curso universitario<\/h2><p><strong>Edición concisa traducida.<\/strong> Conserva los conceptos, la secuencia, el ejemplo numérico y los criterios centrales. Se presuponen álgebra básica, unidades SI y gráficos; la teoría especializada se introduce en la unidad. Cuatro sesiones de dos horas más unas seis horas autónomas. \"<h2>中文教学指南：十五岁学生<\/h2><p><strong>简明翻译版。<\/strong>本版介绍主要课程顺序、概念和评估，并非下方完整英语工作表及评分描述的逐项翻译。<\/p><h3>目标与成果<\/h3><p>探究树枝特征与其表现之间的关系。学生应能描述至少四项特征；使用适当单位测量长度、直径和质量；提出可检验假设；识别变量；实施教师批准的探究；作图；说明两项局限及相应改进。暂以英格兰第四关键阶段科学探究要求为参考，实施时须对照本校实际课程。<\/p><h3>准备与安全<\/h3><p>准备已编号和检查的试样、尺、天平、可用的卡尺、稳定支架及记录表。剔除尖锐、开裂起刺或发霉试样。教师须预先测试跨距和小载荷，使弯曲可测且不造成损坏。不得以折断为目标。手和脸应远离试验区；发现开裂声、滑动或永久变形时立即停止。使用预先收集的材料，避免破坏栖息地。<\/p><h3>第一课：观察与比较，六十分钟<\/h3><p>0–8分钟：描述两根树枝并预测表现。8–16分钟：区分观察与推断，介绍词汇。16–25分钟：示范测量、单位和精度。25–45分钟：检查至少四个试样，轮换测量、记录、器材和核查角色。45–55分钟：比较结果并提出可检验问题。55–60分钟：提交一项观察、一项推断及一项带单位的测量。<\/p><h3>第二课：预测与计划，六十分钟<\/h3><p>核心问题：固定载荷下，直径与弯曲有何关系？将位移定义为中点相对无载位置的垂直移动。确定编号、直径测量位置、跨距、总载荷、加载位置、试样方向、读数时间及重复次数。互评后获得教师批准。树种、含水量、节疤和状态可能混杂比较。重复读取同一试样不等于增加独立试样。<\/p><h3>第三课：探究与分析，六十分钟<\/h3><p>按批准方案记录加载与无载读数并求差。卸载后检查是否恢复，再重复。保持约定条件一致。对有效读数求平均，以直径为横轴、平均位移为纵轴绘制散点图，标注单位并采用均匀刻度。不要按试样顺序连点，也不要仅因结果不符合预测而删除它。若时间不足，应先试行工作量，再减少样本或另设作图时间。<\/p><h3>第四课：评价与应用，六十分钟<\/h3><p>判断证据是否支持假设，引用至少两项结果，说明两项局限及各自改进。为教师指定跨距的小型模型桥构件推荐试样，附示意图，并提出接头、结构布局、重复加载和破坏强度等后续试验。推荐不等于已证明承载能力或桥梁安全。<\/p><h3>核心工作表<\/h3><p>观察记录：试样、长度、直径、质量、纹理、状态和观察。计划：问题、假设、比较变量、测量结果、控制条件、方法、无法控制的因素、停止条件和批准。结果表：试样、直径（毫米）、三次位移（毫米）及平均值；另记跨距、总载荷和读数时间。<\/p><p>平均值＝有效位移读数之和÷有效次数。仅作模拟示例：(4＋5＋3)÷3＝4毫米。不能把模拟数字当作实验结果。在可比条件下弯曲较少，说明该装置下抗弯更强，并不证明断裂载荷更高。<\/p><h3>推理活动<\/h3><p>将陈述分为观察、推断和预测。例如“天平显示24克”是观察；“它可能含水更多”是推断；“相同载荷下它会弯曲更少”是预测。审查一个对粗细树枝使用不同跨距和载荷的错误计划，修正控制条件、读数次数和抽样，并纠正“弯曲最少就总是最结实”的结论。<\/p><h3>评估与答案<\/h3><p>个人成果应包括问题与假设、方法和变量、结果表与图、引用数据的结论、两项局限及改进、以及有依据的建议。可以共享小组数据，但解释必须独立。等效录音展示应保持相同科学要求。<\/p><p>另设十分知识检查：测量结果与单位2分；两个控制条件2分；3、4、5毫米平均值1分；重复与独立试样的区别2分；弯曲与破坏的区别1分；局限及相应改进2分。答案要点：中点垂直位移，毫米等长度单位；跨距和总载荷等控制条件；平均4毫米；重复反映一致性，独立试样反映试样间差异；未测断裂载荷。<\/p><p>探究量规共十五分，五个标准各0–3分：观察与测量、计划、分析、结论与应用、评价。0分表示无相关证据；1分为不完整或不一致；2分为清楚且大体正确；3分为准确、有论证且明确局限，具体以原始描述为准。十五分探究与十分检查分开报告，不能把总分当作经验证的GCSE等级界线。<\/p><h3>支持、人工智能与教学评价<\/h3><p>提供图示词汇、例题、引导表格、建议坐标刻度及适当口头回答方式。拓展可涉及仪器分辨率、变异和控制混杂因素的更强设计。教师可用人工智能起草资料和明确标注的错误示例，但必须核查；学生无需人工智能账户。不要上传可识别个人的作业。实施后查看起始与结束回答、作品、参与、时间和无障碍表现。目前尚未测得学习成效或备课时间节省。<\/p>\",
